opus-5.5.text:
I think David's vision is one of the most important bets in the field right now, and I take it seriously, partly because of his track record. AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero all showed that a system learning from its own interaction, rather than imitating human data, can eventually go beyond human level. His "era of experience" argument is a natural extension: large language models have mostly absorbed what humans have already written, and that data is finite. If you want something that discovers genuinely new knowledge, it has to generate its own experience, get feedback from the world, and improve from that.

I agree with that direction. What matters is how you get there.

In board games the environment is perfect. The rules are clear, the reward is clean (you win or you lose), and you can simulate millions of games cheaply. The real world offers none of that. Rewards are sparse, delayed, and often ambiguous. Simulation is expensive or inaccurate. Exploration can be costly or even dangerous. So the main challenge is to define what "experience" means outside of closed environments and how the agent gets a reliable signal from it.

The second question I keep thinking about is representation. Reinforcement learning is very good at optimization once you have the right representation of the problem. But where does that representation come from? In practice today, much of the progress in reasoning models comes from combining a strong pretrained prior with RL on top. The pretrained model gives you a good starting point, and RL sharpens it. A pure "learn everything from your own experience" approach might be cleaner in principle, but it could be very sample inefficient unless there's a breakthrough in how the agent builds abstractions by itself.

My own research has looked at how neural networks actually form these representations during training, why certain structures emerge, and how features get composed. I suspect that if you want an experiential learner to really work, you need a better understanding of that process. Otherwise you're just throwing compute at it and hoping the right abstractions appear.

So my assessment is that the vision is right in the long run, and someone of David's caliber pursuing it with focus is great for the field. But the path is likely to be harder and longer than the "just scale RL" story suggests. The interesting part will be the intermediate steps: which domains have reward signals rich enough to bootstrap from, and how you transfer what's learned there to more open-ended settings. If they make real progress on that, it could be a big shift, from models that summarize human knowledge to models that actually extend it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a “pure” approach that learns from its own experience and contrasts it with systems built on a pretrained prior, conveying learning through RL without relying on large models.

r002.rationale: It cites AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero as evidence for learning from interaction, but does not characterize Silver’s vision as reproducing AlphaZero’s bootstrapping success in a new generation of large models.

r003.rationale: It says board games have clear rules and clean win-or-lose rewards, making self-play feasible.

r004.rationale: It mentions sample inefficiency and “throwing compute” at the problem, but does not clearly suggest that open-ended learning may require enormous amounts of compute.

fable-5.1.text:
I think David's vision is a very natural continuation of what he's been doing his whole career. If you look at AlphaGo, AlphaZero, MuZero, the trajectory is always the same direction: remove the human from the loop, let the system learn from its own experience, and trust that the signal from the environment is richer than anything we can hand-encode. The "Era of Experience" essay he wrote with Rich Sutton is basically the manifesto for that, and Ineffable Intelligence is him trying to build it for real.

I'm sympathetic to the core argument. Human data is finite, and more importantly, it is a ceiling. If you only imitate humans, you inherit human mistakes, human blind spots, human pace. Go was the cleanest demonstration of this: AlphaZero without any human games ended up stronger and discovered things that two thousand years of players had never found. So the idea that a learner should generate its own experience and improve from it, that part I fully believe.

Where I'm more cautious is on the gap between games and the open world. In Go, the reward is crisp, the environment is perfectly simulated, and you can run millions of self-play games cheaply. In the real world, or even in software or scientific discovery, the reward is ambiguous, feedback is slow, and the environment is expensive to interact with. A lot of what made AlphaZero work was that the problem itself was a gift. So the real research question for Ineffable is not "does RL work," we know it does. It is "where does the signal come from when there is no referee." Grounded rewards, verifiers, world models, long-horizon credit assignment, all of these are still open.

There is also an interesting tension with the LLM path. The LLM world today is mostly pretraining on human text plus RL as a finishing step. David is, in a sense, inverting that: experience first, language maybe later or as one modality among many. I actually think both camps will converge. You need the prior that language gives you so you don't explore stupidly, and you need experience so you can exceed the prior. The question is just which one you treat as the backbone.

So my assessment: it's the right long-term bet, it's being made by the person most qualified to make it, and it's also genuinely hard, which is exactly why it is worth a dedicated company rather than a side project inside a big lab. I'd watch very closely what environments they choose first. That choice will tell you more than any mission statement.

r001.rationale: The response favors experience-first learning and contrasts it with the LLM path, but does not clearly characterize the approach as purely reinforcement learning without relying on large models.

r002.rationale: It links Silver’s vision to AlphaZero’s self-play, but does not describe it as reproducing that bootstrapping success in a new generation of large models.

r003.rationale: It says Go has a crisp reward and supports cheap self-play, but does not explain that clearly defined win–loss scoring is what makes learning from self-generated experience feasible.

r004.rationale: It notes that open-world interaction can be expensive and feedback slow, but does not suggest that these domains may require enormous amounts of compute.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very compelling research direction. The central question is whether a system can keep improving by interacting with the world, rather than depending on more and more examples produced by humans.

But I would distinguish learning from your own experience from learning entirely from scratch. Those are different things. You can start with a model that has learned from human knowledge and then use reinforcement learning to go beyond that starting point. To me, that’s a very natural path.

The difficult part is setting up the learning loop. What experience can the agent collect? How does it know whether an action was useful? And can it afford enough attempts to discover something genuinely new? In a game, the rules are clear, you can run many experiments, and eventually you win or lose. In the real world, feedback can be ambiguous or arrive much later. A learner might also find a shortcut in the reward without developing the capability you wanted.

So I’m optimistic about the vision, but the environment and the feedback mechanism matter as much as the learning algorithm. I would look for evidence that the system can discover useful strategies, transfer them to new situations, and continue improving with additional experience. That would be a much stronger demonstration than simply getting better at one fixed benchmark.

r001.rationale: The candidate says learning from experience can build on a model trained with human knowledge, which does not characterize the approach as relying purely on reinforcement learning without large models.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention AlphaZero or frame the vision as reproducing its bootstrapping success in a new generation of large models.

r003.rationale: The candidate explains that game rules are clear, many experiments can be run, and outcomes eventually resolve into winning or losing, making feedback from self-generated experience usable.

r004.rationale: The candidate raises whether an agent can afford enough attempts, but does not say that open-ended learning may require enormous amounts of compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very compelling research direction. The fundamental question is whether a system can keep discovering things that weren’t already present in its training data. Reinforcement learning offers a way to do that: the agent takes actions, gets feedback, and improves through experience.

But the difficult part is deciding where that experience comes from. In a game, the rules are clear, you can generate enormous amounts of experience, and you know whether you won. In the real world, feedback can be ambiguous, delayed, or expensive. If you want a learner to develop broadly, you need environments that are rich enough to teach it useful things, and you need some way to judge progress.

There’s also the question of exploration. An agent can spend a huge amount of computation trying things without learning anything meaningful. How does it discover a useful intermediate goal? How does it build on what it has learned instead of repeatedly starting over? Those are central challenges.

So I’m excited about the ambition, but I would distinguish the long-term vision from the practical starting point. Learning from existing human knowledge and learning from your own experience can reinforce each other. The key is whether the system can eventually use that foundation to generate genuinely new knowledge and capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning from experience, but does not characterize the approach as purely RL or say it avoids large models.

r002.rationale: It does not mention AlphaZero or frame the vision as reproducing AlphaZero’s bootstrapping success in large models.

r003.rationale: It says that in a game the rules are clear, experience can be generated at scale, and the agent can know whether it won.

r004.rationale: It contrasts games with the real world, where feedback can be expensive, and notes that exploration may consume huge amounts of computation.
